nameStory: The Arrow Clubtail gets its name from the distinctive arrow-like pattern on its thorax, which looks like a pointed arrowhead when viewed from above. Like all clubtails, it also has a swollen 'club' at the tip of its abdomen, giving this dragonfly family its descriptive common name.
description: The Arrow Clubtail is a medium-sized dragonfly with the characteristic clubbed abdomen tip that gives its family its name. These sleek hunters have predominantly black and yellow coloring with distinctive arrow-shaped markings on their thorax. They're streamlined fliers that patrol rivers and streams, often perching on rocks or bare ground along the water's edge. Adult Arrow Clubtails typically measure about 2-2.5 inches long with a wingspan around 3 inches.

idTips.label: Arrow-shaped thorax marking
idTips.description: Look for a distinctive yellow arrow or chevron pattern pointing toward the head on the dark thorax - this marking is crisp and unmistakable when viewed from above

idTips.label: Clubbed abdomen tip
idTips.description: The last few segments of the abdomen are noticeably swollen, creating a club-like appearance that feels rigid if you gently handle a specimen

idTips.label: Bright green eyes
idTips.description: Large, emerald-green compound eyes that shine like jewels in sunlight and feel smooth and hard to the touch

idTips.label: Ground-perching behavior
idTips.description: Often sits directly on sandy or rocky ground rather than on vegetation, remaining motionless for long periods before darting out to catch prey

idTips.label: Yellow and black striping
idTips.description: Body shows alternating bands of bright yellow and deep black that create a bold, contrasting pattern visible even in flight

habitat: Arrow Clubtails prefer clean, flowing rivers and larger streams with sandy or rocky bottoms throughout New England. You'll find them along wooded waterways where there are open patches of bare ground or rocks for perching, especially in areas with moderate current. They favor spots where the water is clear enough to see the bottom and often associate with other stream-dwelling dragonflies.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging from streams in late May, with peak emergence in early June. Look for fresh individuals with shiny wings along rocky stream banks.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity from June through August when adults are most active hunting and mating. This is the best time to observe their distinctive perching behavior on streamside rocks and sand bars.
seasonality.fall: Activity decreases significantly by September, with only a few stragglers visible into early October before the first hard frosts end the flight season.
seasonality.winter: No adult activity - larvae spend winter buried in stream sediments, developing slowly in the cold water until ready to emerge the following spring.

funFact: Arrow Clubtail larvae can spend 2-4 years buried in stream sediment before emerging as adults, breathing through gills in their rectum and extending their lower jaw like a spring-loaded harpoon to catch prey - making them one of nature's most patient underwater assassins.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other clubtails, but the arrow-shaped thorax marking is diagnostic. Remember: 'Arrow points the way' - if you see that distinctive chevron pattern pointing toward the head, you've found your Arrow Clubtail.
contextualKnowledge: The scientific name 'spiniceps' means 'spiny head,' referring to small projections on the head that are visible under magnification. Despite being called 'clubtails,' these dragonflies are actually quite graceful fliers and the club serves as a mating recognition feature rather than any kind of weapon.
compareHints: Arrow Clubtails are distinguished from their Zebra Clubtail cousins by the arrow marking versus zebra-like stripes, and from Riverine Clubtails by their preference for larger streams rather than small headwater brooks. The arrow pattern is unique among New England's hanging clubtails and makes identification straightforward once you know what to look for.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its hanging clubtail relatives, the zebra clubtail stands out with its bold, high-contrast striped pattern - the arrow clubtail has more muted markings with arrow-like shapes rather than stripes, while the riverine clubtail shows more olive-brown coloration with less distinct banding.
